decks.module: Two-second following interval and keeping pace
decks.domain: Backing, Entering Traffic, Roundabouts, Lanes, Speed, Turns, Passing, Stopping and Brakes

cards.front: Why should you keep pace with traffic?
cards.back: Keep pace with traffic, because vehicles moving the same direction at the same speed never collide while moving faster than traffic creates constant conflicts, and if you cannot keep up, move as far right as possible.

cards.front: How do you check your following interval?
cards.back: Striking the vehicle ahead is one of the most common crashes and usually comes from following too closely, so check your interval by noting when the vehicle ahead passes a tree, pole or other marker and counting one thousand one, one thousand two, and if you reach the word two before you reach the marker you have at least the two-second interval you should never go below.

cards.front: What harm comes from tailgating and changing speeds?
cards.back: Following too closely cuts your view of road and traffic conditions ahead, constantly changing speed confuses other drivers and bursts of speed with heavy braking are wasteful and dangerous, so maintain a steady speed.

cards.front: How should conditions and emotions affect your speed?
cards.back: Reduce speed in poor road or weather conditions for better control and more time to react, and never let emotions set your speed, because being in a hurry may mean never arriving at all.

cards.front: How do you use a roadside marker to check your minimum following interval?
cards.back: To check for a safe following gap of at least two seconds, watch the vehicle ahead pass a roadside marker and count one thousand one, one thousand two before reaching that spot.

decks.domain: Backing, Entering Traffic, Roundabouts, Lanes, Speed, Turns, Passing, Stopping and Brakes

cards.front: When is passing justified on two- or three-lane roads?
cards.back: Passing is hazardous on two or three lane roads because the opposing lane must be used and improper procedure can cause a head-on collision, so pass only when the vehicle ahead is moving below the safe speed, never merely because it is there or to gain a few car lengths in moderate or heavy traffic, and in a line of vehicles let those ahead pass the leader first.

cards.front: On which side do you pass, and what is the exception?
cards.back: Pass on the left except when the vehicle being overtaken is making or about to make a left turn, in which case pass carefully on the right but never by driving onto the shoulder, and obey every sign and marking that restricts passing.

cards.front: What are the steps for passing?
cards.back: To pass, keep enough following distance to see opposing traffic, check ahead for conflicting traffic, signal left, physically check behind for anyone passing you, sound the horn so the driver ahead knows, accelerate to passing speed in your own lane, then move left and pass.

cards.front: What should you do if a conflict appears mid-pass?
cards.back: If a conflict appears before the pass is complete, brake sharply and drop back behind the overtaken vehicle instead of speeding up, because speed can be cut more quickly with the brakes than it can be gained with power, and return to your lane only when the overtaken vehicle is visible in your interior rear-view mirror.

cards.front: How do you pass where two or more lanes run your way?
cards.back: Where two or more lanes run in your direction, never use an opposing lane to pass; pass on either side with proper lane change procedure, being extra careful on the right because you approach in the other driver's blind spot, and in every passing situation never pass while approaching or moving through an intersection or crosswalk.

cards.front: What do you do if a conflict appears mid-pass, and what must you not do?
cards.back: When a conflict appears mid-pass you brake and fall back, while speeding up to finish the pass is the move the manual forbids.

cards.front: How does passing a left turner on the right differ from passing on the shoulder?
cards.back: A vehicle turning left may be passed carefully on the right, while passing on the shoulder is prohibited in that same situation.

decks.domain: Backing, Entering Traffic, Roundabouts, Lanes, Speed, Turns, Passing, Stopping and Brakes

cards.front: Which lane do you use with one or two lanes your way?
cards.back: With one lane in your direction you must use it, taking great care in congested areas, and with two lanes in open free-flowing traffic you use the right lane and the left lane only for passing or when vehicles are entering from the right, while in heavy traffic you may use either lane but keep up with traffic at a steady speed without lane hopping.

cards.front: Which lane do you use with three or more lanes your way?
cards.back: With three or more lanes in your direction, choose the center lanes where there are fewer conflicts, leave the right and left lanes for vehicles entering and leaving, keep a steady speed with the flow with few lane changes, and use the right lane if you are slower than other traffic.

cards.front: What checks and signals come before a lane change?
cards.back: Lane changes should be kept to a minimum, and before one you check conditions ahead, to the sides and behind using the mirrors and a physical head-turn check of the blind spots, then signal well in advance, the law requiring a signal for at least one hundred feet before the change begins.

cards.front: How should you move into another lane?
cards.back: With ample clearance, move gradually and steadily into the other lane, because abrupt movements can cause overcontrol or loss of control, and it is better to slow slightly and move in behind a vehicle, keeping it in sight, than to speed up and cut in ahead.

cards.front: Why never force your way into a small gap?
cards.back: Never force your way into a gap at or below the minimum safe following distance, because that discourteous move makes other drivers close ranks against you, whereas allowing time and signaling properly leads courteous drivers to make room.

cards.front: What yielding rules apply when changing lanes?
cards.back: Always yield to vehicles in the other lane when changing lanes, join a congested lane at the end of the line rather than crowding in ahead, stay in your lane until the change can be made safely even if inconvenient, and never change lanes while approaching or moving through an intersection or crosswalk.
cards.memory_hook: Yield, end of line, never intersections

cards.front: How does yielding during a lane change differ from the intersection ban?
cards.back: Changing lanes requires yielding to the vehicles already in the other lane, while changing lanes at or through an intersection or crosswalk is never allowed at all.

cards.front: How does lane choice differ with two lanes versus three or more?
cards.back: With two lanes in open traffic the right lane is the travel lane and the left is for passing, while with three or more lanes the center lanes are the travel lanes and the outer lanes serve entering and leaving traffic.

decks.domain: Backing, Entering Traffic, Roundabouts, Lanes, Speed, Turns, Passing, Stopping and Brakes

cards.front: How do turns differ from curves, and how do you prepare for a turn?
cards.back: Turns are changes of direction from a lane at intersections or driveways while curves are changes in the direction of the road itself, and for a turn you get into the proper lane well in advance, turn from the lane nearest the turn direction into the nearest available lane, and if you are in the wrong lane continue on and turn elsewhere rather than forcing a last-minute lane change.

cards.front: How should you drive through turns and curves?
cards.back: Make precise turns without swinging wide or cutting short, slow to a proper speed before a curve or turn and hold a steady speed through it, because braking or an abrupt speed change in a turn or curve can cause loss of control.

cards.front: Why avoid left turns and U-turns when possible?
cards.back: Avoid left turns and U-turns whenever possible because they conflict more with traffic, are much more hazardous than right turns and impede other vehicles.

cards.front: What do you do while waiting to turn left when the light turns green?
cards.back: When waiting to turn left at a red light and the light turns green, move slowly into the intersection with the wheels pointed straight ahead and turn only when the intersection is clear and it is safe.

cards.front: What should you watch for when turning?
cards.back: Watch with great care for pedestrians, bicyclists and motorcyclists when turning, since vehicles, darkness or weather may hide them, always come to a complete stop before a right turn on a red signal, use extra caution on curves and turns in poor weather or on gravel, sand or mud, and do not drive in a bike lane when turning right at an intersection.

cards.front: How does waiting to turn left differ from turning right on red?
cards.back: While waiting to turn left on green you keep the wheels straight and creep into the intersection, while a right turn on red always begins with a complete stop.

decks.domain: Backing, Entering Traffic, Roundabouts, Lanes, Speed, Turns, Passing, Stopping and Brakes

cards.front: What happens when your wheels slide under hard braking?
cards.back: A hard brake application can make wheels slide, and sliding wheels, especially the front ones, leave you without control of the vehicle.

cards.front: What should you do when about to hit something?
cards.back: When in danger of hitting a vehicle, person or object, do not jam on the brakes and slide the wheels, because you will almost certainly hit it; instead apply and release the brakes rapidly and steer toward a clear area, even off the road, while avoiding people, trees, utility poles and solid structures, and consult the owner's manual for antilock brakes.

cards.front: How do you brake in turns, on slippery surfaces and after water?
cards.back: Avoid braking while turning by slowing beforehand, brake very cautiously on water, ice, snow, frost, sand or gravel, and after driving through water test the brakes and, if they are weakened, apply them lightly several times until normal action returns.

cards.front: What do resting on the brake and a lit brake lamp mean?
cards.back: Resting your foot on the brake pedal lights the stop lamps and misleads following drivers and also partly applies the brakes in many vehicles, causing excessive wear, and a brake warning lamp that lights when you brake means a partial failure needing immediate repair.

cards.front: How should you stop behind another vehicle in traffic?
cards.back: Begin slowing as soon as braking ahead becomes apparent, brake smoothly and steadily, and when stopping in traffic stay far enough back to see where the rear tires of the vehicle ahead meet the road, which leaves room to go around if it cannot move.

cards.front: How do you avoid brake fade from prolonged braking?
cards.back: Prolonged braking heats the brakes and makes them much less effective, which can usually be avoided by shifting to a lower gear so the engine helps hold the speed down.

cards.front: How does braking waste energy and money?
cards.back: Brakes stop a vehicle by turning its energy of motion into wasted heat, so every braking wastes fuel money and wears brakes and tires, and careful braking without bursts of speed followed by hard stops saves energy and money.

cards.front: How does pumping the brakes differ from jamming them?
cards.back: In an emergency without antilock brakes you pump the brakes and steer clear, while jamming the brakes slides the wheels and removes steering control.

decks.module: Backing, driveways and the unattended child law
decks.domain: Backing, Entering Traffic, Roundabouts, Lanes, Speed, Turns, Passing, Stopping and Brakes

cards.front: What does Hawaii law say about leaving a child alone in a vehicle?
cards.back: Hawaii law forbids a driver or any adult passenger from leaving a child under nine years old unattended in a motor vehicle for five minutes or longer, because of dangers such as extreme heat, theft of the car, or accidental use of the emergency brake, power windows or trunk release.

cards.front: How should you check behind before backing?
cards.back: Backing is dangerous because visibility is restricted, so check the area behind the vehicle before getting in, turn around and look to the rear instead of relying on mirrors whose view is too small, and have someone outside guide you if you cannot see.

cards.front: How should you back up safely?
cards.back: When backing, apply the brakes gently as the movement starts to confirm they work, always back slowly, watch the front of the vehicle for clearance when backing and turning at once, and avoid backing into or across a roadway, parking so that you can enter traffic forward.

cards.front: Which lane do you back into, and who must avoid a collision?
cards.back: When traffic is clear, back only into the lane nearest the edge of the roadway, and the chief responsibility for avoiding a collision rests with the driver leaving a parking space, who should look, signal and yield.

cards.front: Why use extra caution backing in residential areas?
cards.back: Use extraordinary caution when backing in residential areas, because children often play behind and between parked vehicles.

cards.front: How must you enter the road from a driveway?
cards.back: Entering from a driveway you must always stop before crossing the sidewalk area, since failing to stop is unlawful, then move forward slowly watching for pedestrians and vehicles, make sure the lane is clear, enter the nearest lane with a right turn when possible, and accelerate to traffic speed.
cards.memory_hook: Stop before sidewalk, then nearest lane

cards.front: How does leaving a parallel space differ from a diagonal space?
cards.back: From a parallel parking space you move forward into the nearest lane when there is enough gap in traffic, while leaving a diagonal space requires backing into the lane first, a much more dangerous and difficult maneuver that takes more time.

cards.front: How does leaving a driveway differ from backing out of a parking space?
cards.back: Leaving a driveway requires a stop before the sidewalk, while backing out of a parking space places the chief collision responsibility on the driver leaving the space.

cards.front: How does leaving a parallel space differ from leaving a diagonal one?
cards.back: Leaving a parallel space is a forward move into the nearest lane, while leaving a diagonal space means backing into the lane, which is slower and more dangerous.

cards.front: How does the unattended child law differ from backing caution?
cards.back: A child under nine may not be left alone in a vehicle for five minutes or more, while children playing behind parked cars are the reason for extra caution when backing in residential areas.

decks.domain: Backing, Entering Traffic, Roundabouts, Lanes, Speed, Turns, Passing, Stopping and Brakes

cards.front: What is a roundabout, and who yields on entry?
cards.back: A roundabout is a one-way circular intersection serving drivers, pedestrians, pedestrians with disabilities and bicyclists, in which entering traffic must yield to circulating traffic, and each approach carries a yield sign and may have yield line markings.

cards.front: How do you drive through a roundabout?
cards.back: Driving a roundabout, slow on approach, yield to pedestrians and bicyclists when entering and exiting, look left and yield to traffic already circulating including bicyclists, drive to the right of the central island counterclockwise at low speed, signal right to exit, and if you miss your exit go around again.

cards.front: How does entering a roundabout differ from exiting it?
cards.back: In a roundabout you look left and yield to circulating traffic, while to leave it you signal with the right turn signal.
cards.memory_hook: Enter yield left, exit signal right

decks.module: Parked cars, stopping in traffic and downshifting
decks.domain: Backing, Entering Traffic, Roundabouts, Lanes, Speed, Turns, Passing, Stopping and Brakes

cards.front: What clues show a parked car may move or open a door?
cards.back: Parked cars block your view of vehicles, bicycles and pedestrians and may pull out or open a door into your path, so watch for movement in or near the vehicle, lit stop, back-up or signal lamps, exhaust smoke or vapor, and turning front wheels, and assume a driver who has just parked will open the door.

cards.front: Why must you not stop unnecessarily in a traffic lane?
cards.back: Stopping unnecessarily in a traffic lane is dangerous, discourteous, inconsiderate and illegal, so stops to load or unload or to talk with others must be made in a parking space, loading zone or other place out of the lane.
cards.memory_hook: Load and talk out of lane

cards.front: When may you enter an intersection or crosswalk?
cards.back: Do not stop within an intersection or crosswalk, and never drive into an intersection or crosswalk unless there is room for your entire vehicle on the far side.

cards.front: What is downshifting, and what does it do?
cards.back: Downshifting means selecting a lower gear range while moving, works with manual and automatic transmissions, and serves two purposes, greater engine braking when slowing or holding speed on a downgrade and better performance when accelerating.

cards.front: When and how should you downshift for a steep grade?
cards.back: Downshift for engine braking before starting down a steep grade because shifting is harder at higher speeds, and on a synchronized manual transmission the procedure is to depress the clutch, move the lever to the next lower gear and release the clutch slowly, while double clutching on a non-synchronized transmission should not be tried without practice.

cards.front: What is the most often listed cause of crashes, and who controls it?
cards.back: Excessive speed for conditions is the most often listed cause of crashes, its underlying cause, whether intoxication, inattention or competition, is controlled directly by the driver, and most vehicles can reach speeds far beyond what the driver, the road and the vehicle can handle.

cards.front: What is a safe vehicle speed?
cards.back: A safe vehicle speed is adjusted to traffic, weather and road conditions and always stays within the posted limits.

cards.front: How does downshifting differ from prolonged braking on a grade?
cards.back: Downshifting before a steep grade lets the engine hold speed, while prolonged braking on the grade overheats the brakes and weakens them.

cards.front: What should you assume about a just-parked driver versus a car showing lamps?
cards.back: A driver who has just parked should be assumed about to open the door, while a parked car showing lamps, exhaust vapor or turning wheels should be assumed about to pull out.
